newsitem.title: UK: British budget - a win-win situation for sterling?.
newsitem.headline: British budget - a win-win situation for sterling?.

text.p: Incredible but true, analysts say the 1997/8 UK budget to be unveiled on Tuesday could offer a win-win opportunity for a traditionally accident-prone sterling.
The pound is currently enjoying a dizzy bull run which has powered it to four-year peaks against the dollar and to 32-month highs versus the mark.

Speculation that interest rates are to rise -- stirred up by a rash of buoyant UK economic data -- have been a major factor in the pound's rally, and those expectations will persist whatever the hue of the budget, currency analysts believe.

"Sterling is really going on its own agenda right now, and I think the budget would have to be very different from expectations to make a dent in it either way," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London. A Reuters survey of 27 economists foresaw a cautious budget with tax cuts of 2.25 billion sterling ($3.79 billion) offset by reduced spending.

"If it's cautious I don't think people will completely jettison the idea of interest rate rises, but I think it'll just make people feel better that the markets are well-placed, the economy's not going to spiral into a boom-bust cycle," said Stephen Hannah, director of research at IBJ International.
The Conservative government, trailing badly in opinion polls and facing a general election within six months, has made it clear it sees tax cuts as a key weapon in the fight for votes.
But the market had been plagued by a fear that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke would spring a tax bonanza that British public finances could ill afford.

That concern -- one of the few remaining negatives for a pound boosted by rate hike expectations, healthy economic fundamentals and bullish technical factors -- was largely alleviated with new public debt data released last week.

Figures showed a flood of corporate tax receipts helped UK government income outstrip expenditure by a massive 4.4 billion pounds in October, the largest debt repayment in any October since records began in 1968.

"I don't think Clarke will go overboard -- he's often said he's a chancellor who won't take risks and good economics is good politics," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London.
Anything fiscally tighter than market expectations should cheer gilts and by extension the currency, said IBJ's Hannah.
"Zero to two billion (pounds of tax cuts) is the sort of range the market will feel comfortable with," he said. "Anything much more than that is the road to ruin."
Even if Clarke confounds expectations with a loose budget, the pound may well reply with a knee-jerk rally, analysts said.
"In the short term it would probably be taken as positive for the currency. The immediate reaction would be that interest rates have to go up," said Deutsche's Barr.

But in the longer term it could be negative. "People might start to get worried about the public sector arithmetic. In the long term it can never be that positive for a currency to run a very strong fiscal deficit," Barr said.
The budget will be a crucial factor in the market's interest rate expectations for the next monetary policy meeting between Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George on December 11.
"If Clarke gives the market a tight budget, he might just get away with not raising rates at all," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
"But it's going to have to be a very credible budget indeed for the market to lose its faith in higher interest rates."
